inline:The proposed evidence cannot distinguish genuine reliability gain from checklist compliance, because a rational checklist-compliant actor who knows the checklist weights or difficulty ordering will also spend more time on harder/critical items, producing the same temporal-complexity correlation.
The problem asks for evidence within a single evaluation that distinguishes a genuine reliability gain from mere checklist compliance that happens to track the right answer. The target asserts that non-uniform effort distribution (time spent correlating with item complexity) distinguishes reliability-driven from compliance-driven actors, claiming 'Compliance-driven actors treat all checkboxes as equal.' But that premise is false: compliance with an explicit checklist does not require uniform time per item. A compliant actor following an explicit, weighted, or difficulty-ordered checklist will naturally spend more time on items flagged as critical or difficult, producing time-spikes on hard items without any genuine engagement with the substantive judgment beyond checking boxes. Thus the evidence is consistent with both hypotheses and fails the distinguishing requirement.
